sql0-t1.title: A query asks the database a question and gets a table back

frames.caption: A table is like one sheet of a spreadsheet. Each row is one thing — one employee. Each column is one fact about it — here, the salary column.
You never open the files. You write a query in SQL and send it. The database first checks that employees, name, salary and dept_id all exist.
It checks every row: is dept_id = 1? Four rows pass. Gus's dept_id is NULL (unknown), so he does not.
It sends back a new, temporary table: only the columns asked for, sorted by name.
The stored table has not changed at all. A SELECT only reads, so it is always safe to run.

sql0-t2.title: The practice database: six tables, two worlds

frames.caption: Six small tables, from two worlds you already know. Every example and exercise in the course uses them, so it pays to know them by heart.

shapes.text: Arrows are foreign keys: each points at the table it refers to.

frames.caption: The company: departments, and employees. Each employee has a dept_id pointing at a department, and a manager_id pointing at another employee (the loop).
Awkward cases are planted on purpose, because real data always has them.

shapes.text: Asha: no manager · Gus: no department · HR: nobody
Ben and Chen earn the same · Hana out-earns her manager

frames.caption: The shop: customers place orders; order_items records which products are in each order, and how many.

shapes.text: An order's amount = the sum of quantity × price over its items.

frames.caption: And the shop's planted cases. Each one is a lesson later on — NULLs, duplicates, missing matches, streaks.

shapes.text: Tom signed up twice · Omar never ordered · Zoe has no city
Order 106: no amount · phone case unsold · Priya: 3 days running

sql0-t3.title: Keys link tables: one-to-many, and many-to-many through a link table

frames.caption: customers.customer_id is the primary key: the values 1 to 6, each used once and never empty, so each one points at exactly one customer.
orders.customer_id is a foreign key: it holds a customer's primary key. Order 101 holds 1, which means "Priya placed this order".
Every order points at exactly one customer. Priya is pointed at five times: one customer, many orders. That is one-to-many, and the foreign key sits on the "many" side.
Nothing points at Omar or the second Tom: they have no orders yet. The database can refuse an order for a customer who does not exist.
An order holds many products, and a product is in many orders. Neither table can hold one id for the other — so a link table, order_items, stores pairs: (order, product, quantity).
Follow order 102: two rows in order_items, pointing at Desk lamp and Backpack. One order, many products.
Now follow product 6, Headphones: rows for orders 101, 104 and 105. One product, many orders. Together that is many-to-many.
order_items' primary key is the pair (order_id, product_id): an order can appear on many rows, and so can a product, but never the same pair twice.

sql0-t4.title: Types decide how values divide, compare and sort

frames.caption: Every column has a type, and the type decides how values calculate. Two whole numbers (INTEGER) first.
An integer divided by an integer gives an integer: 3. The .5 is simply thrown away — not rounded.

shapes.text: 3.5 → 3: the part after the point is dropped

frames.caption: Make one side a decimal and you get the exact answer: 7 / 2.0 = 3.5. CAST(7 AS REAL) / 2 does the same.
CAST changes a value's type: the text '42' becomes the number 42, so + 1 gives 43.
Text compares character by character, left to right — like a dictionary, not like numbers.
The first characters already differ: '1' comes before '9'. So as text, '10' < '9' — the length never gets a look in. Store numbers in number columns.
Dates written as YYYY-MM-DD text are the exception that works: the biggest unit, the year, comes first, so text order is date order.
Character by character, '2022-…' beats '2021-…' at the fourth character. Eli, Hana, Gus pass, in date order.

sql1-t1.title: SELECT picks and calculates columns; FROM says where the rows come from

frames.caption: FROM employees runs first: the database takes every row of the table, with all its columns.

shapes.text: SELECT name, salary, salary + 5000 AS after_raise

frames.caption: SELECT name, salary keeps only the columns you list. The others are simply not in the result.

shapes.text: SELECT name, salary, salary + 5000 AS after_raise

frames.caption: salary + 5000 is worked out separately for every row. AS after_raise names the new column; without it, the column would be called "salary + 5000".

shapes.text: SELECT name, salary, salary + 5000 AS after_raise

frames.caption: One result row for every table row (8), with just these columns. Nothing is saved: after_raise exists only in this result.

shapes.text: SELECT name, salary, salary + 5000 AS after_raise

sql1-t2.title: WHERE keeps the rows where the condition is true

frames.caption: WHERE checks a condition against every row and keeps only the rows where it is true.
First test, dept_id = 1, on each row. For Gus it is unknown (?): NULL = 1 is neither true nor false.
Second test, salary < 90000. Asha passes the first test but fails this one.
AND needs both to be true. Only Ben, Chen and Hana have two ticks. Everyone else is dropped — including Gus, whose "unknown" is not true.
The result: Ben, Chen, Hana. SELECT and ORDER BY then work only on these rows.
With brackets: (dept_id = 2 OR dept_id = 3) is worked out first, then AND salary > 50000.
Department 2 or 3, AND earning over 50000: Dara and Fatima. Eli is in department 2 but earns 45000, so he is out.
Now remove the brackets. AND is worked out before OR — just as × comes before + — so this really means dept_id = 2 OR (dept_id = 3 AND salary > 50000).
Anyone in department 2 now passes, whatever they earn: Dara, Eli, Fatima. Eli is back. Same words, different answer — use brackets whenever you mix AND and OR.

sql1-t3.title: Shorter conditions: a list, a range, a pattern

frames.caption: IN checks a value against a list: status IN ('shipped', 'pending') is true when status equals any value in it.
Each row is compared with the list. Only 105 and 110 match — the same as status = 'shipped' OR status = 'pending', but shorter.
The 10 orders on a timeline from January to March.
BETWEEN a AND b means >= a AND <= b: both ends are included. The range is the 1st to the 29th of February.
Orders 105, 106, 107 fall inside. 106 has no amount, but its date is in range, so it is kept — the filter only looks at order_date.
LIKE matches text against a pattern. % stands for any number of characters (even none); _ stands for exactly one.

shapes.text: WHERE product_name LIKE 'P%' OR product_name LIKE '%s'

frames.caption: 'P%': a P, then anything. Pen and Phone case match.

shapes.text: WHERE product_name LIKE 'P%' OR product_name LIKE '%s'

frames.caption: '%s': anything, then an s at the very end. Headphones matches. (Backpack has no s at the end; Notebook neither.)

shapes.text: WHERE product_name LIKE 'P%' OR product_name LIKE '%s'

frames.caption: OR keeps a name that matches either pattern: Headphones, Pen, Phone case. Everything else is dropped.

shapes.text: WHERE product_name LIKE 'P%' OR product_name LIKE '%s'

sql1-t4.title: NULL is "unknown": = never matches it, and <> quietly drops it

frames.caption: NULL means "unknown". Asha has no manager, so her manager_id is NULL. How do you find her?
manager_id = NULL asks "is this equal to unknown?" — and the answer is always unknown, even for Asha (unknown = unknown is still unknown).
WHERE keeps only rows where the test is true. Nothing is true, so no rows come back at all — and no error tells you.
IS NULL is a real yes/no test. It is true for Asha only: Asha.
"Everyone not in department 1." Gus has no department at all — surely he counts?
For Gus, NULL <> 1 is unknown — not true. So WHERE quietly drops him, even though he is clearly not in department 1.
The result is only Dara, Eli, Fatima. To keep Gus, say so: WHERE dept_id <> 1 OR dept_id IS NULL.
Any arithmetic with NULL gives NULL: 10 + NULL is NULL. Order 106 has no amount, which would spoil any sum you build from it.
COALESCE(a, b, …) returns the first value that is not NULL. For 106 that is the 0; for 107 it is the amount itself, 60.

sql1-t5.title: ORDER BY sorts; LIMIT and OFFSET cut the sorted list

frames.caption: Without ORDER BY, rows come back in no promised order. Here they happen to be in emp_id order.
ORDER BY salary DESC: highest first. Ben and Chen tie on 70000, so their order is not decided yet — either could come first.
The second sort column, name, breaks the tie: Ben before Chen. Now the order is fully decided.
LIMIT 3 keeps the first three rows after sorting: Asha, Hana, Ben. Chen is cut off — even though he earns exactly what Ben earns. "Top 3" can hide a tie.

shapes.text: ORDER BY salary DESC, name LIMIT 3

frames.caption: Pages of 3, sorted by date. Page 1 is LIMIT 3; page 2 must skip the first 3 rows.
OFFSET 3 skips three rows, then LIMIT 3 takes the next three: orders 104, 105, 106. Without ORDER BY, "page 2" would be meaningless.

sql1-t6.title: DISTINCT drops rows that match in every selected column

frames.caption: SELECT location FROM departments gives one row per department: London appears twice.
DISTINCT compares whole rows. The two London rows are identical, so they are duplicates.
One copy of each is kept; ORDER BY then sorts what is left: Leeds, London, Manchester.
Tom signed up twice with the same email. Select name and email: his two rows are identical in every selected column.

shapes.text: SELECT DISTINCT name, email FROM customers

frames.caption: DISTINCT keeps one: 5 rows. Both columns matched, so they count as one row.

shapes.text: SELECT DISTINCT name, email FROM customers

frames.caption: Now select customer_id and name. The two Toms have different ids (2 and 6), so the rows differ — and DISTINCT keeps both. It applies to the whole row, never to one column.

shapes.text: SELECT DISTINCT customer_id, name FROM customers

sql1-t7.title: CASE WHEN: the first true line wins

frames.caption: CASE is SQL's if-else. For each row it tries the WHEN lines from top to bottom and returns the THEN of the first one that is true.
Asha, 95000: salary >= 80000 is true on the first line, so her band is 'high' and CASE stops looking.
Ben, 70000: the first line is false; salary >= 50000 is true, so 'medium'.
Eli, 45000: both tests are false, so ELSE gives 'low'. With no ELSE, he would get NULL.
Every row gets its band. Order matters: if the >= 50000 line came first, Asha would stop there and wrongly get 'medium'.

sql1-t8.title: Row functions: one value in, one value out, for every row

frames.caption: A function takes a value and gives back one value — once for every row. Two rows in department 2: Dara and Eli.
UPPER('Dara') = 'DARA'. Worked out for each row separately.
LENGTH counts characters: 'Dara' has 4.
SUBSTR(name, 1, 3): start at character 1 (SQL counts from 1), take 3: 'Dar'.
Two rows in, two rows out. That is the difference from an aggregate like SUM, which turns many rows into one (Phase 2).

sql2-t1.title: Aggregates: many rows in, one value out — and NULLs are skipped

frames.caption: An aggregate turns many rows into one value. With no GROUP BY, the whole table (after WHERE) becomes one row.
COUNT(*) counts rows, whatever is in them: 10.
COUNT(amount) counts only rows where amount is not NULL: 9. Order 106 has no amount, so it is skipped.
SUM(amount) adds the 9 known amounts: 793. AVG skips the NULL too, so it is 793 ÷ 9 = 88.11 — not ÷ 10.
If the question means "per order, counting the missing one as zero", divide by COUNT(*) yourself: 793 ÷ 10 = 79.3. Same data, different question, different answer.

sql2-t2.title: GROUP BY: one pile per value, one result row per pile

frames.caption: Eight employees, in no particular order.

shapes.text: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id

frames.caption: GROUP BY dept_id puts rows with the same dept_id into one pile. All the NULLs (just Gus) share a pile of their own.

shapes.text: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id

frames.caption: Each pile becomes ONE result row, and COUNT(*) and AVG(salary) are worked out separately for each pile: department 1 has 4 people averaging 78750.

shapes.text: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id

frames.caption: The golden rule: SELECT may only show grouped columns and aggregates. Department 1 has four names — the database cannot pick one for you. And HR has no employees, so no pile and no row.

shapes.text: SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*), AVG(salary) … GROUP BY dept_id

sql2-t3.title: WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after

frames.caption: Two sieves. WHERE filters single rows BEFORE grouping; HAVING filters whole groups AFTER they are counted.
WHERE status = 'delivered' runs first, on rows: 7 of the 10 orders are left.
GROUP BY customer_id makes a pile per customer, and SUM(amount) is worked out per pile.
HAVING SUM(amount) >= 100 removes whole groups: customer 3 (60) fails. Result: customer 1 (275), customer 2 (275). A condition about one row belongs in WHERE — it is cheaper.

sql2-t4.title: Conditional aggregation: SUM a CASE to count several things at once

frames.caption: One pass over the orders, several different counts per customer. The trick: hand SUM a CASE.

shapes.text: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

frames.caption: For each row, the CASE gives 1 if the order is delivered and 0 if not. (Shown here as is_deliv.)

shapes.text: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

frames.caption: SUM adds up the 1s and 0s in each group — which is exactly the number of delivered orders. A second SUM with the opposite condition counts the rest; COUNT(*) counts them all.

shapes.text: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

frames.caption: Swap the conditions for months and the rows become columns — that is a pivot. For a percentage, divide a conditional count by COUNT(*), using 100.0 to avoid integer division.

shapes.text: SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'delivered' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)

sql2-t5.title: The order a query really runs in

frames.caption: You write SELECT first, but the database runs FROM first. Each step works on what the step before it left behind.
2 WHERE salary > 40000 removes rows. Gus (38000) goes: 7 left. WHERE runs before SELECT, so it cannot see SELECT's aliases.
3 GROUP BY dept_id makes piles: department 1 has 4 rows, department 2 has 2, department 3 has 1.
4 HAVING COUNT(*) >= 2 removes whole piles: department 3 goes. HAVING runs after grouping, so it can use aggregates; WHERE could not.
5 SELECT works out the output columns, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary, for each pile that is left. The alias is born here.
6 ORDER BY avg_salary DESC runs after SELECT, so it CAN use the alias. Then LIMIT, if there were one, would cut.

sql3-t1.title: INNER JOIN: keep the pairs that match on both sides

frames.caption: A join pairs rows from two tables wherever the ON condition is true — here, where the dept_ids match.

shapes.text: FROM employees e JOIN departments d

frames.caption: Ben has dept_id 1. Engineering has dept_id 1. That pair matches, so it becomes one result row: Ben, Engineering.

shapes.text: FROM employees e JOIN departments d

frames.caption: Every employee is matched the same way: 7 pairs. Gus (NULL) matches nothing — NULL never equals anything. And no employee points at HR.

shapes.text: FROM employees e JOIN departments d

frames.caption: INNER JOIN keeps only the matched pairs, each with columns from both tables. Gus and HR are simply not there.

shapes.text: FROM employees e JOIN departments d

sql3-t2.title: LEFT JOIN: keep every row of the left table

frames.caption: LEFT JOIN keeps every row of the left table — here departments — whether or not it finds a match.

shapes.text: FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e

frames.caption: Engineering matches 4 employees, Sales 2, Marketing 1. HR matches nobody.

shapes.text: FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e

frames.caption: Matched departments appear once per match. HR still appears — once — with NULL in every employee column.

shapes.text: FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e

frames.caption: Counting per department: COUNT(e.emp_id) skips HR's NULL and gives 0. COUNT(*) counts HR's one NULL-filled row and wrongly says 1.

shapes.text: FROM departments d LEFT JOIN employees e

frames.caption: Step 1: LEFT JOIN customers to orders. Every customer is kept; those with no orders get one row full of NULLs on the orders side.

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON …

frames.caption: Step 2: keep only the unmatched rows: WHERE o.order_id IS NULL. order_id is the orders primary key, so it is NULL only when there was no match at all.

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON …

frames.caption: The customers who never ordered: Omar and the second Tom. That is an anti-join.

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON …

frames.caption: NOT EXISTS says it directly: keep the product if no order_items row exists for it.

shapes.text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi

frames.caption: Notebook: the inner query finds order_items rows, so EXISTS is true and NOT EXISTS is false. Dropped.

shapes.text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi

frames.caption: Phone case: the inner query finds nothing. NOT EXISTS is true: keep it. Result: Phone case.

shapes.text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM order_items oi

sql3-t4.title: A self join compares a table with itself

frames.caption: One table, two aliases: e for the employee, m for the manager. Treat them as two copies of employees.

shapes.text: FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m

frames.caption: Hana's manager_id is 2. In the m copy, emp_id 2 is Ben. So the result row is Hana → Ben.

shapes.text: FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m

frames.caption: Every employee is matched to their manager the same way. Asha's manager_id is NULL, so she matches nobody; LEFT JOIN keeps her anyway.

shapes.text: FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m

frames.caption: The result: each employee beside their manager. With a plain JOIN, Asha would vanish.

shapes.text: FROM employees e LEFT JOIN employees m

sql3-t5.title: Joining three or more tables: follow the keys, and watch the row count

frames.caption: FROM orders (only orders before 22 January, to keep it small): one row per order.
JOIN customers: each order gains its customer's name. Each order has exactly one customer, so the row count stays the same.
JOIN order_items: an order with two items becomes two rows. The grain is now one row per item bought.
JOIN products: each item row gains the product's name. Each JOIN needs its own ON, linking to a table already in the query.

shapes.text: one row per item, with names

sql3-t6.title: FULL OUTER JOIN keeps both sides; CROSS JOIN makes every pair

frames.caption: FULL OUTER JOIN = LEFT JOIN + RIGHT JOIN: every matched pair, plus unmatched rows from BOTH sides.

shapes.text: FROM employees e FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON …

frames.caption: The 7 matched pairs, plus Gus (no department: NULL on the department side) and HR (no employees: NULL on the employee side). It is mostly for reconciling two sources.

shapes.text: FROM employees e FULL OUTER JOIN departments d ON …

frames.caption: CROSS JOIN has no ON at all: it pairs every row of one table with every row of the other.

shapes.text: FROM products p CROSS JOIN departments d

frames.caption: The first product meets every department: 4 pairs.

shapes.text: FROM products p CROSS JOIN departments d

frames.caption: Then the second: 2 × 4 = 8 rows. On its own that is rarely what you want — but it is how you build a complete grid, then LEFT JOIN the real data onto it so gaps show as zero.

shapes.text: FROM products p CROSS JOIN departments d

sql3-t7.title: Two join traps: fan-out, and a WHERE that undoes a LEFT JOIN

frames.caption: Priya's 5 orders, one row each. Their amounts add up to 425.
Join order_items: an order with 2 items now appears on 2 rows — and each row carries the FULL order amount.
SUM(o.amount) now counts 102, 103, 105 and 109 twice: 730 instead of 425. Over all orders it is 1131 instead of 793. That is fan-out.
The fix: sum at the right grain. Total the amounts on orders alone, or aggregate order_items to one row per order (in a subquery or CTE) before you join.
Goal: every customer, with their delivered orders. Put status = 'delivered' in WHERE…

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON …

frames.caption: …and Omar, Zoe and the second Tom vanish. WHERE runs after the join; their NULL status is not 'delivered', so the rows are dropped — the LEFT JOIN has become an INNER JOIN.

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o ON …

frames.caption: Move the condition into ON. It now decides which orders MATCH; every customer is kept, with NULL where no delivered order exists.

shapes.text: FROM customers c LEFT JOIN orders o

sql4-t1.title: Subqueries: one value, a list, or a whole table

frames.caption: A subquery is a query in brackets inside another query. The inner one runs first.
The inner query averages every salary: 63750. It returns one value, so it can go anywhere a single value can.
The outer query now reads, in effect, WHERE salary > 63750. Asha, Hana, Ben, Chen are above the line.
A subquery after IN returns a list: one column, many rows.

shapes.text: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders

frames.caption: The inner query runs first: the customers who ordered in March are 2, 1, 5.

shapes.text: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders

frames.caption: The outer query keeps customers whose id is in that list: Priya, Tom, Zoe. The second Tom (id 6) is not in it.

shapes.text: WHERE customer_id IN (SELECT customer_id FROM orders

frames.caption: A subquery in FROM makes a small table on the fly (a derived table). It needs a name: per_customer.
The outer query treats it like any table — here it averages the totals: 198.25. That is how you aggregate an aggregate.

sql4-t2.title: Correlated subqueries, and why NOT IN breaks on a NULL

frames.caption: A correlated subquery uses a column of the outer row, so it is worked out again for every outer row.
Outer row: order 101, customer 1. The inner query finds customer 1's latest date: 2024-03-10. 101's date is earlier, so it fails.
Order 109, also customer 1: its date equals 2024-03-10, the latest. Kept.
Repeat for every order: each customer's latest order survives — 109, 108, 107, 110.
The subquery lists every employee's dept_id — and Gus's is NULL, so the list contains a NULL.

shapes.text: WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)

frames.caption: HR (4): is 4 NOT IN the list? That means 4 <> 1 AND 4 <> 2 AND … AND 4 <> NULL. The last part is unknown, so the whole AND is unknown — never true.

shapes.text: WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)

frames.caption: So even HR, which nobody works in, is dropped. The query returns no rows at all — and no error warns you.

shapes.text: WHERE dept_id NOT IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employees)

frames.caption: NOT EXISTS asks a different question — "is there any employee with this dept_id?" — and NULLs can't spoil it. Result: HR.

shapes.text: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employees e

sql4-t3.title: A CTE names a step, so the query reads top to bottom

frames.caption: WITH names a step: per_customer is a small table of each customer's total spend, built once at the top of the query.

shapes.text: WITH per_customer AS ( … SUM(amount) AS total … )
SELECT c.name, p.total FROM per_customer p JOIN …

frames.caption: The main query uses per_customer like any table, joining it to customers to get names.

shapes.text: WITH per_customer AS ( … SUM(amount) AS total … )
SELECT c.name, p.total FROM per_customer p JOIN …

frames.caption: It uses the same CTE a second time, to work out the average total: 198.25. With a subquery you would have to write it twice.

shapes.text: WITH per_customer AS ( … SUM(amount) AS total … )
SELECT c.name, p.total FROM per_customer p JOIN …

frames.caption: Keep the customers above the average: Priya (425), Tom (275). Each step can be tested on its own while you build it.

shapes.text: WITH per_customer AS ( … SUM(amount) AS total … )
SELECT c.name, p.total FROM per_customer p JOIN …

sql4-t4.title: A recursive CTE adds rows round by round until a round finds nothing

frames.caption: The anchor runs once: the person with no manager. Asha, level 0.

shapes.text: anchor:    WHERE manager_id IS NULL → level 0

frames.caption: Round 1: the recursive part finds everyone whose manager was found in the last round — Ben, Chen, Dara, Fatima: level 0 + 1 = 1.

shapes.text: anchor:    WHERE manager_id IS NULL → level 0

frames.caption: Round 2: their reports — Eli, Gus, Hana: level 2.

shapes.text: anchor:    WHERE manager_id IS NULL → level 0

frames.caption: Round 3 finds nobody managed by Eli, Gus or Hana. A round with no new rows ends the recursion. Without a way to stop, it would run forever.

shapes.text: anchor:    WHERE manager_id IS NULL → level 0

frames.caption: Anchor: SELECT 1. The CTE starts with one row: 1.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

frames.caption: Round 1: the last row is 1; 1 < 5 is true, so add 1 + 1 = 2.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

frames.caption: Round 2: the last row is 2; 2 < 5 is true, so add 2 + 1 = 3.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

frames.caption: Round 3: the last row is 3; 3 < 5 is true, so add 3 + 1 = 4.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

frames.caption: Round 4: the last row is 4; 4 < 5 is true, so add 4 + 1 = 5.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

frames.caption: Next round: the last row is 5, and 5 < 5 is false — no new row, so it stops. Result: 1 to 5.

shapes.text: SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM numbers WHERE n < 5

sql4-t5.title: Set operators combine two results: stack, dedupe, both, or only the first

frames.caption: Two queries that each return one column of cities. A set operator puts their results together — they need the same number of columns, of matching types.

shapes.text: SELECT location FROM departments ⟨set op⟩ SELECT city …

frames.caption: UNION ALL simply stacks the two results, duplicates and all. It is the fast one: no checking.
UNION stacks them, then removes duplicate rows: 5 different cities are left. Removing duplicates costs a sort or a hash.
INTERSECT keeps the rows found in both results: Leeds and London.
EXCEPT keeps rows of the first result that are not in the second: Manchester has a department but no customer.

shapes.text: SELECT location FROM departments EXCEPT SELECT city …

sql5-t1.title: A window function adds a group's answer to every row, without removing any

frames.caption: Seven employees with a department. We want each one next to their department's average salary.

shapes.text: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg

frames.caption: PARTITION BY dept_id splits the rows into windows, one per department — like GROUP BY's piles. But nothing is squashed.

shapes.text: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg

frames.caption: AVG(salary) is worked out over each window, and every row gets its own window's answer. All 7 rows stay.

shapes.text: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg

frames.caption: Compare GROUP BY: one row per department, and the individual names are gone. A window function keeps the detail AND adds the group's number.

shapes.text: AVG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) AS dept_avg

sql5-t2.title: ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK: three ways to handle a tie

frames.caption: Sorted by salary, highest first. Ben and Chen tie on 70000 — the three ranking functions differ only in how they treat a tie.
ROW_NUMBER: 1, 2, 3, 4… always different. Ben and Chen get 3 and 4; which way round is arbitrary unless you add a tiebreaker (here, name).
RANK: ties share a number, then it skips — like sports. Ben and Chen are both 3, so nobody is 4: Dara is 5.
DENSE_RANK: ties share a number, with no gap. Dara is 4. "The 2nd highest salary" is simply DENSE_RANK = 2.

sql5-t3.title: LAG looks at the previous row; PARTITION BY stops it at the group boundary

frames.caption: One row per month. To compare each month with the one before, a row needs to see its neighbour.

shapes.text: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev

frames.caption: LAG(revenue) looks one row back, in the order set by OVER (ORDER BY month). January has no row before it, so it gets NULL.

shapes.text: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev

frames.caption: Now the change is just revenue − prev: February fell by 235, March by 72. January's change is NULL, because NULL − anything is NULL.

shapes.text: LAG(revenue) OVER (ORDER BY month) AS prev

frames.caption: With PARTITION BY customer_id, each customer's orders are a separate window.
LAG looks back only within the window: each customer's FIRST order gets NULL, instead of borrowing the previous customer's last order. Then days = this date − previous date.

sql5-t4.title: Window frames: running totals, moving averages, and the RANGE trap

frames.caption: With ORDER BY inside OVER, SUM becomes a running total: for each row, the frame is "from the first row up to me".

shapes.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total

frames.caption: Row 2: the frame now covers 2 rows, so the total is 200.

shapes.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total

frames.caption: Row 4: the frame now covers 4 rows, so the total is 445.

shapes.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total

frames.caption: Order 106 has no amount: SUM skips the NULL, so the total stays the same on that row.

shapes.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total

frames.caption: To the last row: 793, the grand total.

shapes.text: SUM(amount) OVER (ORDER BY order_date) AS running_total

frames.caption: A frame can be smaller: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is this row and the two before it — at most 3 rows.

shapes.text: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

frames.caption: Slide down one row: the frame drops the oldest row and takes the new one. AVG over it: 108.3.

shapes.text: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

frames.caption: Slide down one row: the frame drops the oldest row and takes the new one. AVG over it: 131.7.

shapes.text: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

frames.caption: Every row averages its own 3-row window: a 3-order moving average, which smooths out spikes.

shapes.text: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)

frames.caption: The trap: with ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE, which includes every row tied with the current one.

shapes.text: SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) -- RANGE
SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name ROWS …)

frames.caption: Ben and Chen tie on 70000, so with RANGE both rows include both salaries: both show 315000.

shapes.text: SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) -- RANGE
SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name ROWS …)

frames.caption: With ROWS, the frame moves one row at a time (name breaks the tie): Ben 245000, then Chen 315000. Write ROWS when you mean one row at a time.

shapes.text: SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) -- RANGE
SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name ROWS …)

sql5-t5.title: Share of the total, and dealing rows into buckets

frames.caption: Revenue per category, worked out in a CTE first.
SUM(revenue) OVER () — an empty OVER — is one window of every row, so the grand total, 793, is written on every row.
Divide each row by it: Electronics is 100.0 × 440 ÷ 793 = 55.5%. (100.0, not 100, avoids integer division.)
NTILE(4) deals the sorted rows into 4 buckets, like dealing cards. 8 employees, highest salary first.

shapes.text: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name)

frames.caption: The top two salaries go into bucket 1: the top quarter.

shapes.text: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name)

frames.caption: 8 rows ÷ 4 buckets = 2 per bucket. If it did not divide evenly, the first buckets would get one extra.

shapes.text: NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC, name)

sql6-t1.title: CREATE TABLE sets the shape; ALTER TABLE changes it later

frames.caption: CREATE TABLE defines the shape: a name, columns, a type for each, and rules (constraints). It creates no rows.

shapes.text: CREATE TABLE suppliers (supplier_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
name TEXT NOT NULL, country TEXT DEFAULT 'UK');

frames.caption: INSERT (1, 'PaperCo') leaves country out, so the DEFAULT fills it in: 'UK'.
INSERT (2, 'SoundWorks', 'Germany') gives every value, so no default is needed.
ALTER TABLE changes a table that already holds data. products has 7 rows.

shapes.text: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN in_stock INTEGER

frames.caption: ADD COLUMN adds in_stock to every existing row at once, each filled with the default, 1. CREATE and ALTER change the structure (DDL), not the rows themselves.

shapes.text: ALTER TABLE products ADD COLUMN in_stock INTEGER

frames.caption: A SELECT afterwards shows the new column like any other: Headphones and Phone case in Electronics, both in stock.

shapes.text: SELECT product_name, price, in_stock FROM products

sql6-t2.title: Constraints check every write, and refuse the ones that break a rule

frames.caption: subscribers: email is the PRIMARY KEY (unique, never NULL), and a CHECK allows only plan = 'free' or 'pro'. Every INSERT is checked against every rule.

shapes.text: email PRIMARY KEY, plan CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'pro'))

frames.caption: ('priya@mail.com', 'pro'): a new email, an allowed plan. It passes, and is stored.
('tom@mail.com', 'free'): passes too.
('tom@mail.com', 'pro') breaks the primary key: that email already exists. ON CONFLICT (email) DO NOTHING says: skip it quietly instead of failing. Tom stays on 'free'.
Elsewhere: an order for customer 99, who does not exist, breaks the FOREIGN KEY on orders.customer_id. Refused with an error — nothing is changed.
And a department with dept_id 1, which is taken, breaks the PRIMARY KEY on departments. Refused. The rules keep bad data out at the door, not after the fact.

sql6-t3.title: INSERT adds rows, UPDATE changes them, DELETE removes them

frames.caption: Safe habit: run the WHERE as a SELECT first and look at the rows it picks. Here: Dara and Eli.
Then turn it into the UPDATE. SET salary = salary + 5000 uses each row's OLD value to work out the new one.
Only the matching rows change: Dara 65000, Eli 50000. Without the WHERE, every row in the table would get the raise.
DELETE removes the rows its WHERE matches. Tom signed up twice; customer 6 is the duplicate and has no orders.
The row is gone. Because no order points at customer 6, the foreign key allows it; deleting Priya (customer 1) would be refused while her orders exist.
INSERT adds a new row. List the columns, so it is clear which value goes where. The constraints are checked first.

shapes.text: INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, name, email, city…)

frames.caption: Ravi is customer 7. In Leeds there are now: Tom, Tom, Ravi.

shapes.text: INSERT INTO customers (customer_id, name, email, city…)

sql6-t4.title: A transaction is all or nothing: COMMIT keeps it, ROLLBACK undoes it

frames.caption: BEGIN opens a transaction: the following statements become one all-or-nothing unit.
Move Gus into HR. You can see the change, but it is not permanent yet, and other sessions still see the old row.
Give him a raise. Two pending changes now — a crash at this moment would undo both.
COMMIT makes both changes permanent together (Atomic), and once committed they survive a crash (Durable).
BEGIN, then look: order_items has 14 rows.
DELETE FROM order_items — no WHERE, so every row goes. Inside the transaction the table now looks empty.
ROLLBACK throws away everything since BEGIN. All the rows are back, exactly as they were.
SELECT COUNT(*) confirms it: 14. A transaction is your undo button — as long as you have not committed.
Imagine storing everything in one wide table: one row per item Priya bought, with her email and the product's price copied onto each.
Priya's email is stored 9 times. Changing it means 9 updates — miss one and the table contradicts itself.
The same goes for prices: Headphones' price is copied on every line that sold them. Each fact should live in exactly one place.
Normalised: customer facts in customers, product facts in products, and order_items keeps only the keys and the quantity. Joins put the wide view back together when you need it.

sql6-t6.title: A view is a saved query: always current, stores nothing

frames.caption: CREATE VIEW saves a query under a name. It stores no data of its own — only the query text.

shapes.text:
a saved query:
customers LEFT JOIN orders
GROUP BY customer

frames.caption: SELECT from the view runs the saved query on the live tables, then applies your WHERE: Priya 425, Tom 275, Lena 60.

shapes.text:
a saved query:
customers LEFT JOIN orders
GROUP BY customer

frames.caption: Now a new order arrives for Omar: £90.

shapes.text:
a saved query:
customers LEFT JOIN orders
GROUP BY customer

frames.caption: Read the view again: Omar's total is already 90, because the query runs every time. A materialised view would still show his old total until it is refreshed.

shapes.text:
a saved query:
customers LEFT JOIN orders
GROUP BY customer

sql6-t7.title: DELETE removes rows, TRUNCATE empties, DROP removes the table

frames.caption: order_items: 14 rows in a table, like files in a cabinet.

shapes.text: order_items (the table: its columns, keys, indexes)

frames.caption: DELETE … WHERE removes only matching rows, one by one. It can be rolled back. Order 110 has 2 items.

shapes.text: order_items (the table: its columns, keys, indexes)

frames.caption: 12 rows left. DELETE is DML: it changes data, not structure.

shapes.text: order_items (the table: its columns, keys, indexes)

frames.caption: TRUNCATE empties the whole table at once — very fast, no WHERE — but the empty table, with its columns and indexes, stays. (SQLite has no TRUNCATE; DELETE without WHERE does the same job.)

shapes.text: order_items (the table: its columns, keys, indexes)

frames.caption: DROP removes the table itself — rows, structure and all. Querying it now is an error. The database's own list of tables: customers, departments, employees, orders, products.

sql7-t1.title: An index is a sorted copy you can search, instead of reading every row

frames.caption: No index on order_date: the plan says SCAN orders. The database reads every row and checks its date.
CREATE INDEX builds a separate, sorted copy of the dates, as a shallow tree. The leaves hold every date in order; the root holds signposts.

shapes.text: leaves: every date, sorted, each pointing at its row

frames.caption: SEARCH: start at the root. 02-12 is between 01-21 and 03-01, so take the middle branch.

shapes.text: leaves: every date, sorted, each pointing at its row

frames.caption: In that leaf, find 02-12 — it points straight at its row: order 106.

shapes.text: leaves: every date, sorted, each pointing at its row

frames.caption: Three steps instead of reading the whole table. For 100 million rows a B-tree is still only 3–4 levels deep. The cost: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE must update the index too.

shapes.text: leaves: every date, sorted, each pointing at its row

sql7-t2.title: EXPLAIN shows the plan: which table is scanned and which is searched

variants.label: A join, before and after an index

frames.caption: EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN shows how the database will run a query. Each plan line is one table, in the order it is read: the first is the outer loop.

shapes.text: SELECT c.name, o.amount FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON … WHERE c.city = 'Leeds';

frames.caption: Before indexing orders.customer_id: SCAN o reads all 10 orders, and for each one SEARCHes customers by its primary key, then checks the city.

shapes.text: SELECT c.name, o.amount FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON … WHERE c.city = 'Leeds';

frames.caption: After CREATE INDEX on orders(customer_id), the plan flips: SCAN c (only 6 customers, 2 in Leeds), then SEARCH o USING INDEX for each Leeds customer.

shapes.text: SELECT c.name, o.amount FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON … WHERE c.city = 'Leeds';

frames.caption: Read plans for three words: SCAN (a whole table — fine if small, a red flag if big), SEARCH … USING INDEX (good), and TEMP B-TREE (a sort or grouping — costly on big data).

shapes.text: SELECT c.name, o.amount FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON … WHERE c.city = 'Leeds';

sql7-t3.title: Index-friendly filters: keep the column bare, and use the leftmost column

frames.caption: An index on order_date keeps the dates sorted. Here they are, in index order.
WHERE strftime('%Y-%m', order_date) = '2024-02': the index is sorted by the raw date, not by strftime(date). The database must work out the function for EVERY entry: SCAN.
Rewrite it so the bare column is compared with values: a range. Now the database jumps to the first February date and reads until March: SEARCH.
A composite index on (customer_id, order_date) is sorted by customer, then by date within each customer — like a phone book: surname, then first name.
customer_id = 1 AND order_date >= '2024-02-01': the leftmost column is fixed, so the matches sit side by side — one jump, then read: SEARCH.
order_date >= '2024-02-01' alone skips the leftmost column. The matching dates are scattered across every customer, so the index can't be searched: SCAN. That is the leftmost-prefix rule.

sql7-t4.title: Three ways a database runs a join

frames.caption: Nested loop: for each row of the outer table (order_items), look up its match in the inner table (products) — by index, so each lookup is a quick search.
Item 1 needs product 6: one index search finds it.
Item 2 needs product 4: one index search finds it.
Item 3 needs product 5: one index search finds it.
…and so on for every outer row: about N × log M work. Without an index on the inner side, every lookup would read the whole inner table: N × M.
Hash join, step 1 (build): read the smaller table, products, into a hash table — each row goes into a bucket chosen from its product_id.
Step 2 (probe): stream the bigger table past it. Each order_items row works out its bucket and looks only there.
One pass to build, one pass to probe: about N + M, with no index needed — but the hash table must fit in memory.
Merge join: both inputs sorted by product_id. Walk them side by side, like closing a zip.
Left is at product 2; move the right pointer forward until it reaches 2: a match. Neither pointer ever moves back.
Left is at product 4; move the right pointer forward until it reaches 4: a match. Neither pointer ever moves back.
Left is at product 6; move the right pointer forward until it reaches 6: a match. Neither pointer ever moves back.
One pass over each input: about N + M — if they are already sorted (by an index, say). Otherwise each must be sorted first.

sql8-t1.title: Five steps for any SQL question

frames.caption: Question: "Which city brings in the most delivered revenue?" Step 1: say it back and ask — delivered only? Customers with no city? Ties?

shapes.text: "Which city brings in the most delivered revenue?"
delivered only?  no city → drop or "unknown"?  ties?

frames.caption: Step 2: look at the data before writing the answer — 10 orders, 4 customers who ordered, 1 order with no amount. Know the grain: one orders row is one order.
Step 3: plan out loud — "first the delivered orders, then join each to its customer's city, then total per city, then sort."

shapes.text: delivered → join city → group by city → sort

frames.caption: Step 4: write it as small CTEs, one step each, running each one as you go.

shapes.text: SELECT city, SUM(amount) … GROUP BY city

frames.caption: Step 5: check a number by hand. London = Priya 275 + Lena 60 = 335. Then say the edge cases and how your query handles them.
